text: My name is Jediah and I joined Cursor early in 2025 as the longest tenured engineer working on our agent harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And recently I came along to SpaceX as part of the acquisition of Cursor.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So today I want to talk to you all about how the agent harness has evolved to where we are today and where I think things are going.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And there's a motivating question that I have for us to answer today, which is, is the agent harness dead?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's get started.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here's a more natural and flowing version of that script which reads like a cohesive conference talk rather than a series of short points.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Oops.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Just making sure everyone's still got their slop detectors on before lunch.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: No, for real.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the story starts in early 2023 when Prompt Engineer was the hottest title out there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: By mid-2025, that had evolved to context engineer, someone who programmatically puts the best context for the model together on the fly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then only at the beginning of this year did the industry land on the term agent harness and harness engineering to describe work that my team and I have been doing for a while.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what's in an agent harness?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The harness is like the eyes and the hands for the model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It wraps around the model, steers it, and connects it to the world.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Users connect to our harness through apps, and then the harness connects the model to computers and also to third-party services like MCPs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I like to divide the harness into two layers, the runtime and the context and orchestration layers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The runtime is kind of like the foundation of the harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It controls where the core agent loop runs and how state is stored so that work can resume.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Building this foundation is a lot like traditional software engineering.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then the context and orchestration layers are kind of like the Wild West.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is what a lot of people refer to when they talk about the harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These parts of the harness control which models are called when and what context they see.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That includes things like prompts and tools, of course, but also memory, compaction, and a bunch of tricks you might not know that we do to make the agent behave in the way that we want.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is the area that I primarily work in.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In the new year, we kind of hit peak harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Cursor announced that we had created a browser entirely from scratch using a new long-running harness called Grindswarm.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This was a multi-model harness that orchestrated a lot of agents and a lot of machines, and it was very expensive to run.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It actually took down Cursor maybe once or twice to get this demo.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like anything in the world of agents, it only took a few months of peak harness for people online to start saying that the harness was dead.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Tariq from Anthropic talked about how they had killed much of the system prompt from Claude Code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Gary Tan from YC thought that the harness would fade away and only skills would matter.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Even myself and my colleague Stefan, we wrote about how we had removed all these guardrails that we had in Cursor to patch over gaps in the model's intelligence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We used to have things like a small model just to apply code edits to a file because the frontier models weren't good at this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We also had all sorts of coding-specific instructions like how to explore the code base and how to check your work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So if all these people were saying the harness is dead, they were saying that smarter models are what killed it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And there's a lot of evidence for that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I want you all to think about a very simple harness where the model only has access to the shell and to all of my secrets.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Please don't screenshot this slide, by the way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This one's off limits.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So who here thinks that this really simple harness would do just as well on coding evals as a more sophisticated one?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Maybe some hands.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Who thinks it would?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Raise your hand if you think it would.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A few hands.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Most of you know.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A few recent studies tried to investigate exactly that question.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first one, out of UC Berkeley, tried seven different frontier models on a series of harnesses including Py, Codex, and Claude Code.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what they found, particularly on the newer, smarter models, is that the choice of harness did not actually make a difference significantly in the score on SweetBench Lite.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then another study from Apple and EPFL found similarly that a dedicated MLE harness did not make a big difference on an MLE bench.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what is going on here?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Is it actually true that the harness is dead?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Are they right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here's what I think that the evidence shows.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A fancy harness in this day and age no longer adds coding intelligence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I think that is true.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I know that's surprising.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But these things that we used to do in the harness to patch over gaps in the raw coding muscle memory of the model, like teaching it how to explore the code base, how to work persistently for a very long time with things like slash goal, how to run tests to check your work, the model has natively absorbed these skills.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So why is this happening?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It turns out the harness is actually making itself obsolete through what I call the data flywheel.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So in this process, the harness brings harder and harder coding tasks within reach.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: At that point, more users can productively attempt those tasks with agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That means more coding data is shared with the labs.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And eventually the models learn natively how to do these skills well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Eventually,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The models get so good that the harness can actually delete the things it needed to do to make those tasks work in the first place.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a very interesting process.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that's how you get people saying that the harness is dead.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if the models are good enough to code well in any harness, then why should you care?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Does it really matter which harness you use?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Is the harness really dead?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I say no, and there's two reasons why.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First of all, and I'm going to go into both these points, the harness actually opens the new frontier of tasks for the model to solve.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then second, there are some tasks or some parts of the harness, especially outside the context layer, which the model cannot absorb.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So to first talk about how the harness unlocks the next frontier, I want to talk about GrokBot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Who here has tried GrokBot?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Can I see some hands?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Awesome.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Let's go.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's great.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So for those of you who haven't, GrokBot is our autonomous colleague who gets work done for you, not just coding, but all kinds of knowledge work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I really recommend you try it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm not going to sell too much, but it's a groundbreaking new product.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's already created a new category.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Let's just talk about the harness, though.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So Grokbot has a new kind of harness that operates not based off of one-off chats, but long-lived coordinator bots that orchestrate a fleet of worker agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can kind of think of it like hiring a high-powered lawyer who deals with you directly and own strategy, but they farm out their tasks to a team of paralegals.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's like that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, something interesting about the GrokBot harness is I mentioned how in Cursor we found ourselves removing things from the harness, removing prompting, removing guardrails as the models got smarter.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But curiously, in GrokBot, we've actually found ourselves putting back a lot of these things, adding new prompting, adding new guardrails.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that's because there's a lot of new tasks in this new way of working, in the new domains that GrokBot is meant to solve, that the models have not nailed yet.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: To give a few examples of those kind of things, just a few things that we're focused on right now when it comes to GrokBot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's key website flows like making slide decks and booking travel, communication.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: An autonomous colleague needs to keep you up to date on what it's been doing without overwhelming you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Acting versus asking is another big one.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: GrokBot can do a lot of things which are kind of risky in some sense, like emailing your colleagues.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You want to be able to do that, but you only want it to do it in the way that you intended.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then, of course, learning over time the way that you work through memories is another big focus.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So those of you who might have pushed the boundaries with coding agents might have noticed that none of these tasks are new.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But for GrokBot, they're much more important because everybody is needing them in some way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And right now in GrokBot, it is the harness that is making these tasks feasible.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Of course, the model is a big part of that, but the harness is helping bring them within reach.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So going back to our data flywheel, GrokBot, that example, lets us fill in the last arrow in our cycle, which is when a capability like coding gets commoditized by the model, it's actually the harness which unlocks a new frontier for the model to then solve and kicks off that flywheel again.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that might look like taking on new tasks outside of the coding domain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As we just saw with GrokBot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Or it could just mean taking on tasks in the software engineering job beyond pure coding.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm sure some of you here are pretty senior in your software careers, and you might know the more senior you get, the less coding you're actually doing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So there's a lot of other things in the job that matter.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is the core idea that I would like you to understand.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This flywheel and how the model and the harness together drive it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One more example of how the harness can unlock new frontiers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some of you may have heard of this idea of the software factory, where you have multiple agents coordinating together to solve the full software development lifecycle.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, this is far from a solved vision, but there's a lot of innovation happening across the industry at the harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: To give an example of how this might manifest internally, we have a lot of channels where someone might report a bug to that channel, and then an automation immediately auto triages that bug.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then it might kick off a cloud agent to try to fix the bug, and that agent will use our tooling to show before and after videos to prove that it's fixed.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then once that fix is deployed or is merged and starts deploying, we have our rollouts product, which kicks off another agent to watch in production for any issues.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you can think of all this as almost like a meta harness, which is orchestrating many agents together.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That's how I would like you to think about this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that's the first reason that you should care about the harness, because a frontier harness is needed to be at the frontier of agentic tasks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then the next reason is there are some parts of the harness that the model can't absorb.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's talk about those.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First of all, there is the infrastructure and runtime needed to make an autonomous colleague reliable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Over the past year plus, we've gone from agents that work on a typical task for minutes to hours to days and even longer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And there's just no way that this can work on one person's laptop, which might go to sleep.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has to be running in the cloud if you really want an autonomous colleague.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then next, we have trust and security.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Yes, like we saw before, a simple harness with just bash and all your API keys in a file can solve coding tasks, but you probably don't want to give all your API keys in a file to the model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Or if you're OK with that, I'm sure that your head of security would have something to say.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is obviously really important.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Companies where we want to have permissions that are scoped down to specific agents and specific people.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But it's also important to have guardrails for anyone who doesn't want to wake up one morning to a really catastrophic action or to a $10,000 API fee, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then finally, there's efficiency.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you think back to those two studies I showed where the choice of harness did not make a significant difference in eval scores, both of those studies actually found that there was a significant difference in cost per task.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I have personally been focused over the past month on optimizing the efficiency of the GrokBot harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, through tweaking variables like cache hit rate, improving that, token efficiency, model mix, we were able to bring down the costs and the speed of GrokBot significantly for users without any hit to quality.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Users have really, really been appreciating this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's been awesome to see.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It could be an entire different talk about how we did this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the key takeaway here is that the more and more that you use agents to do your work, the more it matters, the more valuable it will be for you to have the most efficient harness.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So by now, you might be convinced that the harness still matters.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then you might be asking, what's next?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here's a few trends that I'm anticipating.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First of all, that flywheel is speeding up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And right now, we've entered a new age where the product is once again moving faster than the model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That means that the harness is going to get more messy before it gets cleaned up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There's going to be more things shipped.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So because of this, we're expecting people to build their harnesses, design them so it's easier to ship and unship new features.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One way we're already seeing that manifest is with both GrokBot and other similar products, less and less of the harness inner workings are being exposed to the user.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Some of you may have heard of Hiram's Law, which says that anything that you expose to users, they will come to depend on.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, obviously there are trade-offs to giving users less visibility into what's happening.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But one advantage is that there's less change management to deal with, and you can iterate much faster.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, another way that we've been seeing this trend manifest is a bigger focus on designing primitives for agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Primitives are like building block interfaces that can be composed and extended into powerful features.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When you have primitives, you can add new features without making things more complicated for the agent, and you can remove features without having to do a complicated refactor in your codebase.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's just good engineering.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One example across our agent harnesses of a primitive we've added is called subscriptions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agents need a way to wake up in response to events.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Those might be someone posting in Slack, CI going red on a PR that the agent cares about, or just a certain time of day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, rather than having separate integrations for each of these things, we have one framework and one tool that the model can use or the agent can use to subscribe to an event.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then another cool thing that we do, I mentioned earlier that we have these deterministic guardrails to patch over bad behaviors in the model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That might be, for example, if GrokBot doesn't respond to the user fast enough, and we might give it a little nudge and say, hey, user's waiting on you.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We'd rather not do these things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're kind of like hacks.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But we would rather fix them now than wait for the next model checkpoint to get released.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So in order to make our codebase be less messy and have less of a worse time iterating the future, we track all these things, which we call shims centrally.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And every time the model uses one, it gets logged.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So now we have a bot who watches this dashboard.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And whenever a shim stops firing, that model or that agent will put up a PR and say, this shim can be cleaned up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Another thing that I think is next for the harness is it is moving up to a higher level of abstraction.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Yesterday's generation of harnesses were built from composing a bunch of LLM calls.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now the new harnesses we're seeing, like GrokBot and the Software Factory, are using agents as the core building block.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then finally,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I predict that within six months, 90% of agent work is going to run off the laptop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is already where things are going.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And I think there's just no way that this is not necessary in order to have truly autonomous agents who can really work with us in the way that we want.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So is the harness dead?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The parts that made it smarter at coding?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Yes, that is the flywheel at work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That is the flywheel at work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the harness, as we saw, is how the agents can unlock the next frontier of work.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then also the trust, the efficiency, the infrastructure that the harness brings, those things are not going anywhere.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So yesterday's harness may be dead, but long live the agent harness of tomorrow.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Thank you.
